entities.name: Quintus Servilius Caepio
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Servilius Caepio, a prominent Roman *nobilis* of the late 2nd century BCE, is primarily remembered for his disastrous consular command in 106 BCE and proconsular year in 105 BCE, culminating in the catastrophic Battle of Arausio. This defeat, one of the most severe in Roman history, exposed profound fissures within the Roman military and political elite, particularly concerning the command structure and the rivalry between patrician *nobiles* and *novi homines*. His actions directly contributed to the political instability that facilitated Gaius Marius's subsequent military reforms and unprecedented rise to power.

Elected consul in 106 BCE, Caepio was dispatched to Transalpine Gaul to confront the Cimbri and Teutones, Germanic tribes who posed a significant threat to Roman territory. He achieved an initial success by recovering the gold of Tolosa, which he allegedly embezzled. In 105 BCE, as proconsul, he was ordered to cooperate with the plebeian consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus. Caepio, a proud patrician, vehemently refused to serve under or even camp near Maximus, whom he viewed as an inferior *novus homo*. This deep-seated rivalry and egregious lack of coordination led to the two Roman armies, numbering perhaps 80,000 legionaries and auxiliaries, being annihilated separately by the Cimbri and Teutones near Arausio (modern Orange, France) on October 6, 105 BCE.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Quintus Servilius Caepio's catastrophic failure of command at Arausio led directly to the loss of 80,000 Roman soldiers and catalyzed the critical Marian military reforms, fundamentally altering the nature of the Roman army and its role in the Republic's collapse.
